Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

France 24. BBC. Reuters. Al Jazeera. Washington DC. Human Rights Watch.

When does a government stop calling it foreign interference and start asking, why is the entire world saying the same thing about us?

Here is what is actually happening inside India right now:

▪️ India has the world’s strictest content takedown window; just 3 hours. No major democracy, and no major authoritarian regime, moves this fast against its own citizens’ speech.

▪️ Under the new IT Rules 2026 amendment, it’s not just news outlets being targeted. Ordinary users, influencers, and anyone who simply shares a news post can now fall under the government’s content blocking framework.

▪️ The Internet Freedom Foundation has formally called this “digital authoritarianism” and a “dangerous expansion of executive power.” These are not opposition politicians, these are constitutional lawyers and digital rights experts.

▪️ Since 2014, India’s government takedown orders have surged 14 times; from 201 to 14,775. And post 2022, this data was denied under RTI on grounds of national security.

▪️ Meta alone was forced to restrict 28,000+ pieces of content in India in just the first six months of 2025; following government orders.

▪️ India currently ranks 151 out of 180 in the World Press Freedom Index. We are sitting between countries most Indians would be ashamed to be compared with.

▪️ The Supreme Court’s own Shreya Singhal judgment; a landmark free speech ruling, is being systematically bypassed by these rules. 

This is not policy. This is contempt of constitutional precedent.

The government will say this is about deepfakes. About national security. About public order.

But when 138 YouTube videos were taken down for allegedly defaming Adani, a private businessman, it stopped being about security a long time ago.

France 24 is not attacking India. France 24 is holding up a mirror.

The question is, why is this government so terrified of what Indians might see in it?

Statement : SBI has told the stock exchanges about its data breach, but not the customers whose data was leaked

New Delhi, 21 October 2026

Today, the State Bank of India told the BSE and the National Stock Exchange, in a disclosure under Regulation 30 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, that it has experienced an incident involving the loss of customer data. On 16 October 2026 the bank received alerts from its threat intelligence service provider, the Defence Cyber Agency and CERT-In that its customers’ data was available on the dark web. Its preliminary analysis of about 3.75 lakh records found 3,897 customer records containing personal information. These include registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, names, gender, email addresses, residential addresses, branch and CIF identifiers, lead IDs and details linked to loan records. The bank says it does not yet know where the data came from, and it has engaged a CERT-In empanelled agency to find out.

SBI did not detect this breach itself and learnt of it from outside agencies after the data had already been published. On the same day, a threat monitoring account on X flagged a claim by a group calling itself “Siriusim” that it had released 3.75 lakh rows of SBI data and 2,722 PDF documents, including loan applications and account opening forms. The bank’s disclosure does not mention these documents. It also does not say what the remaining records, beyond the 3,897 it has identified, contain.

At the time of this statement, SBI has not said that it has informed any of the affected customers, and its disclosure is silent on the point. Five days passed between the alert and today’s filing. The filing assures investors that the incident has no material impact on the bank’s operations, financial performance or business continuity. However, it does not state anything to the 3,897 people whose phone numbers, dates of birth and home addresses are now with fraudsters. These customers are the most likely to receive calls from persons posing as SBI officials who can recite their account details back to them. A customer cannot guard against a fraud she has not been warned of.

The Internet Freedom Foundation calls on SBI to inform every affected customer directly and without further delay.

We regret to note that the law in force today does not compel the bank to do so. Section 8(6) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires a Data Fiduciary to intimate a personal data breach to the Data Protection Board and to each affected Data Principal, and Rule 7 of the DPDP Rules, 2025 prescribes how this is to be done. But the Union Government chose a staggered commencement, and these provisions will take effect only on 13 May 2027, nearly four years after Parliament enacted the law. The reporting obligations that apply today, under the CERT-In Directions of 28 April 2022 and the RBI’s cyber security framework for banks, are owed to regulators and not to customers. A listed bank is bound to keep the stock exchanges informed. No law in force clearly binds it to inform the people whose data it holds.

Our demands

1. SBI must inform each affected customer by SMS, email and letter to the registered address, in English, Hindi and the language of the customer’s branch, stating what data was exposed and what steps they should take. It should open a dedicated helpline and an online facility for customers to check whether their data is affected.

2. SBI must state what the 3.75 lakh records and the 2,722 documents contain, how many customers they relate to, and whether they include KYC documents such as Aadhaar, PAN or passport copies.

3. When the investigation concludes, SBI must disclose how the data left its systems, including whether it came through a vendor or a direct selling agent, and publish a summary of the investigating agency’s findings.

4. The Reserve Bank of India should direct all regulated entities to notify customers of personal data breaches within a fixed period, pending the commencement of the DPDP Act.

5. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology should bring Section 8(6) of the DPDP Act and Rule 7 of the DPDP Rules into force immediately.

text: 🚨 Indian Government asks Meta to review Facebook and Instagram algorithms to prevent misleading content and ensure users aren’t exposed to only a limited set of narratives. https://t.co/sTMrjCxl3B

ONE GOVERNMENT BLOCKING ORDER EVERY 68 SECONDS — IS INDIA'S DIGITAL DEMOCRACY UNDER THREAT?

Pause for a moment. In the five months from March to July 2026, nearly 1.95 lakh government-backed blocking orders were sent to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, according to data reported by The Indian Express.

That is approximately 1,275 orders every day. One every 68 seconds.

This is not a trivial administrative statistic. It raises a fundamental democratic question: who decides what citizens are allowed to see, discuss and criticise online?

🚨 THE NUMBERS DEMAND PUBLIC SCRUTINY

* Instagram received nearly 1 lakh orders.

* Facebook received around 80,000.

* YouTube received nearly 15,000.

* Meta's two platforms—Instagram and Facebook—accounted for roughly nine out of every ten orders directed to these three platforms.

For comparison, RTI information previously reported by The Indian Express showed 2,312 blocking orders sent through the Sahyog portal to 19 platforms between October 2024 and October 2025.

The scale of the subsequent increase deserves a detailed public explanation.

THE MOST DISTURBING QUESTION: CAN A MACHINE REMOVE OUR VOICE WITHOUT MEANINGFUL HUMAN REVIEW?

According to The Indian Express, Meta integrated its API with the government's Sahyog portal to comply with a shortened takedown deadline. The report says this enabled government-flagged content to be removed automatically, without a separate human review by the company.

Automation may make administration faster. But speed is not the same as justice.

What happens if an order is mistaken, overbroad or insufficiently justified? Who checks whether the content actually violates the law? How quickly can an ordinary citizen challenge the decision and restore lawful speech?

A system that can silence first and explain later needs exceptionally strong safeguards.

📢 WHY THIS MATTERS TO EVERY CITIZEN

The reported orders coincided with student protests against examination-paper leaks at Delhi's Jantar Mantar. The reporting also described takedowns affecting posts concerning the government's ethanol-blending policy and the West Bengal elections.

The presence of a takedown order does not, by itself, prove unlawful censorship. Governments have legitimate duties to address unlawful content, and the law permits restrictions in defined circumstances.

But criticism of the government, peaceful protest, investigative journalism and political disagreement must not be casually treated as threats merely because they are uncomfortable for those in power.

India's constitutional commitment to freedom of speech cannot survive on assurances alone. It requires lawful orders, transparent procedures, independent scrutiny and effective remedies.

⚖️ THE LAW MUST NOT BECOME A SHORTCUT AROUND DUE PROCESS

The reporting distinguishes the takedown mechanism associated with Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act from the separate blocking framework under Section 69A.

These are not interchangeable provisions. Their legal basis, procedures and safeguards matter. The public deserves clarity about which authority issued each order, what legal grounds were invoked and what opportunity affected users had to challenge it.

OUR DEMANDS

1. Publish regular, platform-wise statistics on government takedown orders, their legal grounds and their outcomes.
2. Ensure meaningful human and legal review of disputed or ambiguous directions.
3. Give affected users clear notice, subject to narrowly justified exceptions, and an effective appeal mechanism.
4. Disclose the safeguards governing automated integration between government portals and social-media platforms.
5. Ensure that peaceful dissent, journalism and legitimate political criticism are not suppressed through vague or overbroad directions.
6. Enable independent judicial scrutiny wherever legality or fundamental rights are contested.

India cannot call itself the world's largest democracy while treating transparency about restrictions on public speech as optional.

THE ISSUE IS NOT WHETHER GOVERNMENTS CAN ENFORCE THE LAW. THE ISSUE IS WHETHER THEY CAN DO SO WITHOUT ACCOUNTABILITY.

A democracy must protect citizens from unlawful content—but it must also protect citizens' right to question the state.

When posts disappear, citizens deserve to know why. When orders are issued, the public deserves to know under what authority. And when lawful speech is wrongly removed, there must be a meaningful remedy.

Digital India must not become a system in which technology makes silencing citizens easier than answering them.

This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

On 22 September 2026, IFF filed RTI applications with MoRTH and NIC asking who has access to VAHAN, SARATHI, e-Challan and PUCC data. NIC’s reply of 16 October discloses that 25,314 credentials were issued to private entities and that 17.08 million queries were run through them in 33 months. It also says private sharing was discontinued from 1 October 2026 on MoRTH’s directions, a decision we have found announced nowhere. (1/8)

Read More: https://t.co/ky7ppU9Hlc

Ending private sharing is a welcome step, but it was done without a public order, a Gazette entry or a news report. An arrangement switched off without a stated reason can be switched back on the same way. We still don’t know why it was ended, whether recipients must delete the data they already hold, or whether this is permanent. Meanwhile, the ₹29 app is still live on the Play Store, with 10M+ downloads, as of 17 October. (6/8)

The switch-off covers only private entities. Under clause 4.3 of the NTR Policy, police and law enforcement agencies keep complete access to every field, including personal data, with no consent or judicial check. In Delhi, this access underpins the Safe City camera network, the ANPR cameras at border points and e-Challan. It will also underpin the ₹1,789.52 crore Intelligent Traffic Management System approved on 30 September, which will be integrated with VAHAN. (7/8)

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

1. Settings → Wi-Fi → tap (i) next to your network

4. Add 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1
5. Save

For mobile data: install the "1.1.1.1: Faster Internet" app by Cloudflare from App Store. It sets up a system-wide profile.

WINDOWS 11 / 10

1. Settings → Network & Internet → Wi-Fi (or Ethernet)
2. Click your active connection
3. Scroll to "DNS server assignment" → Edit
4. Change to Manual → toggle IPv4 on
5. Preferred: 1.1.1.1 | Alternate: 1.0.0.1
6. Save

Press Windows key → type "cmd" → right-click "Command Prompt" → Run as administrator → Yes. Black window opens. Type ipconfig /flushdns, press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
macOS

1. System Settings → Network
2. Click your active connection → Details
3. Click DNS in sidebar
4. Click + and add 1.1.1.1, then 1.0.0.1
5. Remove existing ISP entries (select, click −)
6. OK → Apply

Open Terminal: press Cmd + Space → type "Terminal" → Enter. Copy-paste sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder, press Enter, type your Mac password (invisible while typing, that's normal), press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ROUTER (covers every device on Wi-Fi)

1. Open 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1 in browser
2. Login (credentials usually on router sticker)
3. Find DNS settings (under WAN, Internet, or DHCP)
4. Primary: 1.1.1.1 | Secondary: 1.0.0.1
5. Save and reboot router

Best option if you want laptop + phone + smart TV + everything to work without per-device setup.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
VERIFY IT WORKED

Open browser: visit https://1.1.1.1/help

It'll confirm you're using Cloudflare DNS + whether DNS-over-HTTPS is active. Then try polymarket(dot)com

━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Some ISPs use Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) or SNI-based blocking. In that case:

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

Your app didn’t crash because of a bug. It crashed because the Indian government decided to block your backend.

Starting February 24th, https://t.co/cpotyIe5BS became unreachable across major Indian ISPs. Supabase later confirmed this was due to a ministry order. No prior notice. No public explanation. No transition window.

Jio. Airtel. ACT Fibernet. All started DNS-poisoning Supabase domains, redirecting API calls to a sinkhole IP. Every app running on Supabase in India (auth, database, edge functions, real-time) went dark for millions of users. Reports suggest Firebase Hosting is facing similar disruptions.

Thousands of startups, student projects, hackathon builds, production SaaS apps. Blocked. No “here’s 90 days to migrate.” Nothing.

Supabase had to publicly tag Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw on X just to get someone to talk to them: “Supabase is used by millions of developers worldwide, and millions of users in India are currently unable to access our platform. Could we talk to someone in your team about this?”

Silence from MeitY. Silence from the Minister. Silence from every ISP.

Supabase is not a social media platform. It’s a PostgreSQL database wrapper with auth, storage, and APIs. Its users are engineers building software. There is no obvious legal or content-based reason to block it.

And this isn’t the first time. Medium blocked on Jio/Airtel in Oct 2025. Linktree blocked without explanation. BSNL blocked Dailymotion and Telegram links in Aug 2025. ACT Fibernet blocked TheMovieDB. Ubuntu mirrors and Cloudflare R2 hit before that.

Critical internet infrastructure keeps getting caught in opaque, unaccountable blocking orders. No public reasoning. No appeals process. No distinction between a piracy site and a developer tool.

The workaround? Switch DNS to 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8. Use a VPN. Proxy backend traffic through custom domains so you’re not exposed to ISP blocks.

But think about what we’re saying. We’re telling Indian developers: “Your government might randomly block your backend, so architect around that.” That’s not a healthy ecosystem. That’s building on a minefield.

We talk about Digital India. Startup India. A $5 trillion economy. We want to compete globally in SaaS and AI.

But we’re blocking the tools our developers need to build. Without notice. Without reason. Without a plan.

India’s builders deserve better than this.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

#Bhiwandi Police Bust Online Betting Racket, Arrest 10; 32 Mobiles and 46 ATM Cards Seized

Bhiwandi (#Thane), October 23–24: Bhoiwada Police in Bhiwandi have uncovered an online betting and financial fraud network, arresting 10 accused during a raid in #Mumbai’s Aarey Colony area. The action followed a complaint by a local resident who was allegedly lured with a work-from-home job offer.

During the raid, officers seized 32 mobile phones, 46 ATM cards, 40 SIM cards, four laptops and other materials.

The arrested persons have been remanded in police custody. Officials said the investigation is continuing to trace the absconding mastermind and uncover the full extent of the network. Some reports also link the broader police action to a second network involving the illegal trade of codeine-based drugs, in which additional arrests were made.

Police have warned citizens not to hand over bank accounts, ATM cards or SIM cards to strangers under the guise of job offers.

🔗 This is the full 2018 debate for anyone who wants to see Lucas and her war on merit: https://t.co/w7iGZqXnnW

FAST FORWARD: "GREED" vs. MERIT
Federal prosecutors allege one Lucas, used her political office as part of a years-long operation to sell marijuana, launder the proceeds — and ultimately turn Virginia’s legalization of recreational marijuana into what she allegedly called “generational wealth," not through merit but by allegedly cheating the system.

The 45-page federal indictment names names: 
❌ Louise Lucas
❌ Her daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke
❌ Her daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb
❌ Her grandson Ryan Eichelberger
❌ Businessman Prince Albert William Hudson III 
❌ Businessman Carlton Upton Jr.
❌ Businesswoman Tameka Johnson

Prosecutors allege the “Lucas Enterprise” operated from at least 2019 -- two years before the debate on merit -- and pursued two intertwined objectives: 
❌ Distributing marijuana
❌ Using Lucas’ political influence to shape Virginia marijuana policy and obtain valuable recreational licenses

Here is the extraordinary chronology prosecutors laid out, in their own words. 

RISE TO POWER
Lucas was elected to the Virginia Senate in 1991 and rose to become chair of the powerful Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee and Senate President Pro Tempore.

According to the indictment, her family operated The Cannabis Outlet in Portsmouth.

💰 Her daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke allegedly handled business affairs and attended meetings.
💰 Her daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb allegedly managed the store.
💰 Grandson Ryan Eichelberger allegedly worked in its day-to-day operations.

Prosecutors say Lucas was explicitly warned.

After a senior law-enforcement officer was hired in 2022, the indictment says he warned Lucas that selling marijuana was illegal and “was going to get her in trouble one day.”

At another meeting, the officer allegedly asked why, “given that she was a state senator and a wealthy woman,” she would engage in criminal behavior.

According to prosecutors, Lucas didn't answer.

By then, prosecutors allege marijuana was already moving through the family business.

2022: 'FREEDOM IS DOPE'
In early 2022, prosecutors say an alleged supplier identified ICC #1 contributed $15,000 to the 420ish Unity Festival, partly organized by Lucas.

The receipt allegedly described the payment as:

“Freedom is Dope.”

Then, on April 19, 2022, Lucas and daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke allegedly met ICC #1 at Lucas’ office.

The indictment says that between June and July 2022, an alleged supplier identified as ICC #1 delivered between THREE AND FIVE POUNDS of marijuana to The Cannabis Outlet.

Lucas allegedly paid between $3,500 and $4,000 IN CASH.

'VIRGINIA FREEDOM LIFE'
According to the indictment, Lucas asked ICC #1 whether he was a member of law enforcement before discussing marijuana prices.

That same day, daughter Lucas-Burke allegedly wrote a $6,600 check to ICC #1 from Virginia Freedom Life.

It bounced.

Lucas allegedly replaced it with another $6,600 check from Backyard Entertainment.

By fall 2022, prosecutors allege the business was operating at scale.

Between fall 2022 and early 2023, ICC #2 allegedly sold The Cannabis Outlet “multi-pound quantities of marijuana totaling approximately 100 pounds” for $100,000-$150,000.

Prosecutors say Lucas, through daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb, paid $52,000 in checks and the remainder IN CASH.

Then came the texts.

'THE LUCAS LADIES'
On Oct. 3, 2022, prosecutors say Lucas texted the alleged supplier:

“Good morning … this is to confirm the time for our meeting at the store today. I am so excited and looking forward to seeing you”

And:

“we (The Lucas Ladies) love doing business with you”

'I'M GOING TO NEED MORE FLOWER'
Daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb allegedly texted with the supplier about the mechanics of marijuana sales.

One message described packaging and selling “half ounces (14)” and “ounces (28).”

Another allegedly said:

“you can keep going on the blend if you can’t keep up with sativa and indica.”

Days later:

“Good morning. I’m going to need more flower.”

The money trail continued.

The indictment lists payment after payment from The Cannabis Outlet to Prince Albert William Hudson III, whom prosecutors describe as a marijuana supplier.

💰 December 2023: more than $21,000.
💰 January 2024: more than $26,000.
💰 February: more than $29,000.
💰 March: $129,000.
💰 April: $132,000.
💰 May: $125,000.
💰 June: $123,000.
💰 July: more than $79,000.
💰 August: $91,000.
💰 September: $67,000.

And investigators weren't merely watching.

💰 On Oct. 4, 2024, and Oct. 18, 2024, the indictment says law enforcement made CONTROLLED PURCHASES of marijuana from The Cannabis Outlet.

More controlled buys followed.

💰 On May 5, 2025, an undercover officer allegedly bought 10.2 grams of marijuana from The CBD Shoppe.

💰 By 2025, prosecutors allege payments continued flowing to Hudson and another alleged supplier, ICC #1.

The indictment records tens of thousands of dollars month after month.

Meanwhile, daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb allegedly received a series of $2,500 payments from an Agri-Carter account controlled by Hudson.

Then investigators intercepted a shipment.

On Aug. 13, 2025, Norfolk police seized SEVEN POUNDS OF MARIJUANA allegedly shipped to High-N-Wellness in Norfolk.

According to prosecutors, payments and marijuana transactions nevertheless continued.

By October 2025, law enforcement was buying directly from The Cannabis Outlet again.

💰 Oct. 23, 2025: controlled purchase of ½ ounce.
💰 Oct. 31, 2025: controlled purchase of one ounce.

During that transaction, prosecutors say Eichelberger told the undercover officer another load of “product” was due Nov. 3.

'THE ELECTION' 
Then came a text prosecutors put directly into the indictment.

On Nov. 15, 2025, Lucas allegedly wrote about “the election” and told ICC #2:

“you know I will be carrying the legislation as the Chief Co-patron.”

She allegedly proposed sitting down to discuss “how about we begin with you sending at least a good faith payment of the money you owe me…”

'LIST OF STUFF FOR YOU TO TRY'
In January 2026, prosecutors say the operation moved directly into Lucas’ legislative office.

Grandson Ryan Eichelberger allegedly began texting businesswoman Tameka Johnson asking for “a lil have a list of stuff for you to try & get for next time.”

Then: “can you get the COAs for the flower and other products?”

💰 On Jan. 30, 2026, according to prosecutors, Lucas asked ICC #2 to come to her office at the Capitol complex in Richmond.

💰 There, the indictment says Lucas provided “partial repayment” of money ICC #2 had paid for an interest in Mama’s Chicken, LLC.

💰 Then Lucas allegedly asked ICC #2 to provide marijuana “samples.”

💰 The next day, Jan. 31, 2026, prosecutors say Lucas and ICC #2 met AGAIN — this time at her legislative office in Portsmouth.

Lucas allegedly called in daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke and grandson Ryan Eichelberger.

They discussed sources of marijuana.

When Eichelberger asked whether the cannabis was hemp, prosecutors say ICC #2 replied:

“[I]t’s not hemp, it’s THC.”

'GET GENERATIONAL WEALTH'
Then prosecutors allege Lucas explained the endgame.

After the conversation, Lucas and ICC #2 allegedly continued discussing marijuana and marijuana licensing.

According to the indictment, Lucas said obtaining a license was a way for her to:

“get generational wealth and this is my last chance.”

The alleged undercover operation kept going.

💰 Feb. 3, 2026: ICC #1 allegedly arrived at The Cannabis Outlet with “a large bag” from his vehicle and took it inside.

💰 Feb. 5, 2026: controlled purchase of 69.5 grams from The CBD Shoppe.

💰 Same day: controlled purchase of 116 grams from High-N-Wellness.

💰 On Feb. 9, 2026, prosecutors say Lucas called ICC #2 and discussed the recreational-marijuana legislation pending in the General Assembly.

The indictment quotes Lucas:

“this is our last chance at generational wealth . . . I’ve got too old to not be greedy.”

Two days later, law enforcement allegedly observed ICC #2 throwing a white trash bag into a dumpster.

Investigators recovered it.

The indictment says the bag contained marijuana packaging bearing “the odor of marijuana.”

March 2026: prosecutors allege the political and business sides increasingly converged.

Lucas allegedly told grandson Eichelberger and businesswoman Tameka Johnson to find additional marijuana sources.

Then, prosecutors say, Lucas telephoned another Virginia legislator and explained why she needed a marijuana license.

The alleged quote is stunning:

“I got to get the license and I got to get the money rolling because I want — I want to make generation, create some generational wealth.”

She allegedly continued:

“I need to be covered under his (UPTON’s) um, hemp license.”

On March 11, 2026. prosecutors say Lucas participated in another call with Virginia legislators and daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke about recreational marijuana licenses.

Lucas allegedly said:

“we trying to disqualify somebody [UCC #2] until he pays me back my money.”

March 31, 2026: Businessman Carlton Upton Jr. allegedly met Lucas at her Portsmouth office.

“I only got five licenses, but you know what I mean, you first, so I need to talk to you before I make any decisions that affect you.”

💰 April 23, 2026: prosecutors say Lucas called a member of the Virginia Cannabis Control Authority and asked whether there was anything the official could do for her.

💰 According to the indictment, Lucas said she needed “to invest in something that — that can help me generate some uh, generational wealth for my family.”

Then came the raids.

💰 May 6, 2026: Federal search warrant at The Cannabis Outlet — marijuana recovered.
💰 Federal search warrant at The CBD Shoppe — marijuana recovered.
💰 Federal search warrant at Hudson’s Exotic World in Danville — marijuana recovered.
💰 July 10, 2026: Law enforcement returned to The Cannabis Outlet for another controlled purchase.
💰 Agents bought two strains labeled “Sativa” and “Indica.” According to the indictment: Both tested positive for marijuana.

The grand jury ultimately charged an alleged racketeering conspiracy involving Lucas, daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke, businessman Prince Albert William Hudson III, grandson Ryan Eichelberger, daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb and businessman Carlton Upton Jr.

Prosecutors say the alleged enterprise sought to obtain and illegally distribute marijuana AND procure “generational wealth” for its members.

The indictment goes further.

Prosecutors allege the enterprise used business entities to disguise marijuana proceeds and used Lucas’ political influence “to insulate the Lucas Enterprise from state law enforcement actions.”

They also allege her influence was used to pursue marijuana licenses that could financially benefit the enterprise.

Prosecutors describe Lucas as the alleged “leader of the enterprise.”

They accuse her of approving and directing criminal activities, arranging marijuana acquisition and distribution, supervising laundering of marijuana proceeds and using her political influence in an effort to shape Virginia legislation for herself and her family.

The indictment contains EIGHT COUNTS, including allegations involving:

❌ Racketeering conspiracy
❌ Conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute marijuana
❌ Money laundering conspiracy
❌ Honest-services fraud conspiracy
❌ Maintaining drug-involved premises
❌ Possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug-trafficking crime
❌ Wire fraud

The charges vary by defendant.

One of the most consequential allegations isn't simply that marijuana was illegally sold.

Prosecutors allege Lucas used her elected office to advance the financial interests of herself, her family and associates as Virginia debated creation of a potentially lucrative recreational marijuana market.

The honest-services count alleges a scheme to deprive Virginians of Lucas’ “intangible right” to her honest services.

The indictment alleges Lucas invested money with ICC #2 in an entity positioned to benefit from marijuana licensing, did not report that interest on required Statements of Economic Interests, and later demanded a partial $100,000 repayment while continuing to work to direct a license to ICC #2.

These are allegations. An indictment is not proof of guilt, and every defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty. 

That's the position that Sen. Surovell, the lawmaker who pushed the legislation to remove merit from Virginia's No. 1 high school, is taking as he stands by her in support against the indictments.

The government has now laid out, in extraordinary detail, its theory of how an alleged marijuana business, a family network, money and political power converged over years.

And prosecutors repeatedly return to the phrases they attribute to Lucas herself: creating "generational wealth" by being "greedy."

I hope the telling of this story will give you a wider window into why this case captures not only the crossroads that a politician faces of success through merit or through cheating but also the questions that a nation faces: to go down the path that this lawmaker allegedy supported of shortcuts and dishonor or to choose a path of honor, merit and hard work. 

In 2021, Lucas silenced parents who believed in merit and hard work. 

Today, in 2026, she is facing serious charges for violating "honest-services" laws, money laundering, wire fraud and racketeering.

text:
In a First for India, Karnataka Cyber Command Busts Illegal eSIM Box Syndicate; 4 Held After 55-Day Hunt

​Bengaluru

In a landmark operation marking the first such case cracked anywhere in the country, the #Karnataka State Police #CyberCommand Unit has busted an illegal embedded SIM (#eSIM) box network operating clandestinely out of two residential apartments in the Whitefield tech corridor, officials confirmed on Thursday.  

​The breakthrough came after an arduous, nearly 55-day technical pursuit. Unlike conventional physical SIM cards that leave direct point-of-sale footprints and visible hardware trails, tracking virtual eSIM profiles across encrypted networks presented severe investigative challenges. Investigators had to pierce through layered digital provisioning pipelines before finally closing in on the syndicate's infrastructure and supply chain.  
​Four key operatives linked to the illicit procurement and conversion of eSIMs have been arrested from Tiroda in #Maharashtra’s Gondia district.  

​The 55-Day Investigation and Bust
​The probe began after the Chief Circle Nodal Officer of Bharti #Airtel Limited, #Bengaluru, lodged a complaint on August 26, 2026, flagging suspicious, unauthorized routing over Airtel connections in the Whitefield and Kadugodi pockets. The #Whitefield #CyberCrime Police Station (CCPS) registered  and set the technical hunt in motion.  

​Because the syndicate deployed virtual eSIM profiles rather than traditional physical SIM cards, pinpointing the hardware locations and device identities required extensive cyber forensics and telemetry analysis in close coordination with the Department of Telecommunications (#DoT), Karnataka.  

​Following nearly two months of sustained tracking, joint teams raided two high-density operational hubs functioning in separate apartments within the Whitefield division:  

1. ​Kadugodi Facility: Six SIM Box (GSM gateway) units housing 32 slots each, totaling 192 slots active with provisioned eSIM connections across multiple telecom service providers.  

2. ​Pattandur Agrahara Facility: Four SIM Box units with 32 slots each, accounting for 128 active slots.  

​Operating in tandem, the dual facilities wielded a combined capacity of 320 live lines running through a single coordinated network. The setup functioned as an illicit domestic exchange, masking international originations and routing unauthorized traffic to bypass telecom firewalls and lawful interception systems.  

​Tracing the digital breadcrumbs behind the virtual profiles led cyber investigators to Tiroda in Maharashtra’s Gondia district, where operatives were procuring SIM credentials and converting them into activated eSIM profiles to feed the Bengaluru gateways remotely.​Four accused persons, all residents of #Tiroda, were tracked down and arrested; however, police have withheld their identities citing the ongoing investigation.

​According to police, the country-first eSIM box setup served as the core telecommunications backbone for widespread cyber intimidation schemes nationwide, including infamous "#DigitalArrest" scams, sextortion rackets  and high-value financial fraud.  

​"Preliminary leads suggest the possibility of substantial financial exposure, potentially running into hundreds of crores of rupees across the wider network," said Dr. Pronab Mohanty, IPS, Director General of Police, Cyber Command. "The actual number of victims, financial losses, and the full extent of the network remain subject to verification through continuing investigation and inter-agency coordination."  

​Forensic analysis of the seized gateway hardware and cloud logs is underway to map out every call routed through the hub and uncover the masterminds directing the syndicate.

text:
I'm on a plane to Ireland tonight. Tomorrow a man goes on trial for a tweet.

I'm writing this from the airport. In a few hours I'll be in the air, and tomorrow morning I'll be sitting in the public gallery of Bray District Court, south of Dublin, for the trial of Kirk Loco.

You may remember Kirk. He's an ordinary Irishman. Two years ago someone in that group posted a warning: a migrant man had exposed himself on a public bus, in front of a 14-year-old girl. The bus driver stopped the bus. There were half a dozen witnesses. It was on CCTV.

Kirk did what any of us would do. He reposted the warning so other parents would know.

The migrant wasn't charged. Kirk was.

The Irish police charged him under a so-called "fake news" law, Section 12A of the Criminal Justice Act, 1976. It was passed during the Troubles to fight terrorist propaganda. It had never been used against anyone, in fifty years, until they used it on Kirk. He is the first and only person in Irish history to be prosecuted under it. They picked him because of his politics: he's a critic of mass immigration. They are making an example of him.

Here's what has happened since. Kirk has been dragged into that courtroom in Bray again and again, almost ten times, for a single retweet. Each time he takes a day off, each time his lawyers prepare, each time the Gardaí (that's what the Irish call their police) turn up and the thing gets put off again. I've flown over for one of those hearings myself. In May the judge lifted an outrageous bail condition that had banned Kirk from attending any protest, anywhere in Ireland. That was a real win. But the same judge refused to order the police to hand over the bus CCTV or the names of the witnesses. The people who saw what happened on that bus could clear him in five minutes, and the state won't tell his lawyers who they are.

Kirk said it best himself: "I just can't believe that I'm eight court appearances in for a retweet." That was in May. There have been more since.

The process is the punishment. Even if Kirk wins tomorrow, he's already been punished for two years: the stress, the lost days, the cloud over his name, the ban on protesting. That's the point. It's not really about convicting Kirk. It's about making sure every other Irish person who sees something on a bus thinks twice before saying a word.

Tomorrow is finally the trial itself. A full day. Kirk's barrister, Laoise de Brún, and his solicitor, Padraig Langsch, will fight it in open court. They are principled lawyers who refused to do what Irish legal aid lawyers do, which is tell you to plead guilty, pay the fine and go home. Kirk won't plead guilty to telling the truth.

And then I'm staying on. Because four days later, on Tuesday, the same two lawyers are back in court in Wexford, for Hugh Fagan. Hugh is the man I wrote to you about this week: he sits quietly on a bench in his town square with homemade signs, wearing headphones, and for that he's charged with a public order offence. Same country, same pattern, same week. One man for a tweet, one man for cardboard.

I'm going alone this time, no videographer, economy flight, cheap hotel, to keep the costs down. I'll live-tweet from inside both courtrooms (I'll be the only journalist there; RTÉ never shows up) and I'll film my own reports outside on the courthouse steps and send them to you the same day.

Ireland's "fake news" law had never been used on anyone until Kirk Loco. If they get a conviction, it becomes the template. That's why this one trial matters far beyond one man.

Kirk's trial is Friday, October 23 in Bray. Hugh Fagan's is Tuesday, October 27 in Wexford. One trip, two trials.

text:
🚨 Exposing a brand in India? 

Before you post, you need to know if they can actually get your video taken down for speaking your truth."

[Do Not Skip This Part]👇
Note: This tweet is only for general understanding of how this happens. A recent tracking down of a video involving the brand has occurred. Here is a thread to understand how it happens. Please refrain from mentioning the brand name or creator name in comments or replies to this tweet. 
 
In India, there is no simple rule allowing a brand to remove a video simply because it criticizes the brand. 

The usual route is a mix of:

IT Act + IT Rules + platform policy + civil court injunction/defamation/commercial disparagement suit.

1) What is the core legal structure?

Platforms like YouTube, X, Instagram, etc. are treated as intermediaries. They get “safe harbor” protection for user-generated content, but they may lose that protection if they ignore valid legal directions.

Under India’s intermediary framework, a platform gets legally strong “actual knowledge” mainly through:

A court order, or
A government/authorized agency direction/intimation

A private brand complaint alone usually does not automatically force a platform to remove a video. 

The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India - clarified that platforms should not be forced to decide legality merely based on private complaints; the stronger trigger is a court order or government direction.

2) How does a brand complaint become a court order?

The structure usually works like this:

Step 1: The brand's legal team collects evidence

The company gathers the video URL, transcript, screenshots, claims made in the video, alleged false statements, impact on reputation, possible business loss, and proof of harm.

Step 2: The brand's legal team may send a legal notice

This is often the first pressure step. The brand may demand a takedown, an apology, a correction, damages, or the removal of specific claims.

Step 3: The brand files a civil/commercial suit.

If the creator does not comply, the brand can file a case for defamation, commercial disparagement, trademark issues, unfair trade practice, or reputational/business harm.

Step 4: The brand asks for urgent interim relief

The brand may request an interim injunction, sometimes ex parte, meaning the court can issue a temporary order without first hearing the creator if it believes urgent harm may occur.

Step 5: The court checks the matter prima facie

At this stage, the court is not finally deciding who is right. It checks whether there is an arguable case that the content may be false, misleading, malicious, defamatory, or commercially disparaging.

Step 6: The court may pass an injunction

The order can direct the creator to remove the video, stop sharing it, stop repeating certain claims, or restrain publication of similar allegedly disparaging content.

Step 7: The court order is sent to the platform
Once YouTube/X/Instagram receives the order, the platform may remove or disable access to the video to comply and protect its intermediary safe harbor.

3) Does the brand need to contact the platform grievance officer?

They can, but for defamation or brand-disparagement disputes, the platform may not want to act purely on the brand’s private complaint unless the violation is very clear under platform policy.

The more powerful route is:

Brand → Court → Court order → Platform compliance

The grievance officer becomes important when the platform receives a complaint, legal notice, or court/government order. But the grievance officer is not usually the final judge of whether a review is defamatory or fair criticism.

4) Can a video be removed just because it criticizes a company?

No. Criticism alone should not be enough.

A creator can usually criticize a product, company, service, pricing, quality, privacy policy, design, marketing claims, or consumer experience.

But risk increases when the video makes strong factual claims, such as:

“this phone is fake”
“this company is cheating customers”
“this is just a rebranded phone”
“do not buy this because the company is lying”
“this brand is a scam”

These claims need proof. If the creator presents them as facts and the company says they are false, misleading, malicious, or damaging to business, the company may go to court.

5) What does the court usually look at?

For a temporary injunction, the court may consider:

Prima facie case: Is there an arguable case that the content is false, misleading, defamatory, or commercially disparaging?

Balance of convenience: Who will suffer more harm if the order is or is not granted?

Irreparable harm: Can the damage to reputation or business be fixed later with money, or is immediate restraint needed?

Proof and testing: Did the creator rely on reliable documents, technical tests, expert analysis, official sources, or only assumptions?

Language used: Was the tone fair and analytical, or aggressive and conclusive without enough proof?

6) What can the creator do after an ex parte order?

The creator can challenge the order in the same court. 

They can ask the court to vacate or modify the injunction and argue that:
the video was fair comment,
the claims were based on evidence,
the company suppressed facts,
the order was passed without hearing the creator,
the takedown is too broad,
or public interest requires the video to remain available.

7) Practical creator lesson

A review video is safer when it clearly separates:

Opinion: “In my view, this looks like poor value.”

Fact: “The model number matches X device.”

Evidence: screenshots, teardown, software logs, official filings, import data, product pages, privacy policy, benchmark/test method.

Limitations: “Based on my testing,” “I could not independently verify X,” “the brand has been contacted for comment.”

The danger zone is when the creator makes a strong factual allegation without showing a reliable testing method or source.

Important point:
Fair criticism is not illegal. But factual claims like “fake phone”, “rebranded phone”, “scam”, “company is cheating” need strong proof.

Disclaimer: I have shared only how the law is applied in such cases; this tweet does not reflect my opinion or view on any similar incident. 

Bookmark this for the future; this will be useful for a lot of creators out there.

text:
A friend of mine is being buried in paper.

His adversary keeps filing complaints against him with different authorities, one after another. Each complaint runs from 150 to 900 pages.

Every page sounds plausible. The allegations are structured, logical and full of references, and almost all of them are baseless.

That doesn't matter, though, because each one has to be answered.

Filing a complaint costs his adversary almost nothing. Answering it costs my friend lawyers, weeks of document collection, replies, hearings and appearances. Then the next complaint arrives at another authority, and it starts again.

His legal bills are enormous, and he hasn't done anything wrong.

This is the future of legal work in India, and most people are looking the wrong way.

There's an old idea called Brandolini's law: the effort needed to refute nonsense is an order of magnitude bigger than the effort needed to produce it.

AI has just made producing it nearly free.

A few years ago, a 900-page complaint needed a team and real money. Today, one angry person with a chatbot can produce it in an afternoon, polished, cited and convincing to anyone who doesn't check every line.

Generating allegations costs almost nothing. Refuting them is still expensive, and that asymmetry is going to reshape Indian legal practice.

Everyone keeps asking which legal jobs AI will kill. Routine drafting, contract review and friendly deals will shrink, because when both sides want the same standard outcome, AI gets there quickly.

But where one side wants to hurt the other, AI is a weapon, and weapons create work for the defence.

Here is where I think work will increase for Indian lawyers:

1. Defending against complaint warfare
Multi-forum complaints to police, regulators, tax authorities, professional bodies, consumer forums and RERA. Someone has to read, analyse and answer every one of them, and that work grows fastest.

2. Quashing and stopping abuse of process
Petitions under Section 528 BNSS (old 482 CrPC), writs against mechanical show-cause notices, and applications to club, stay or transfer proceedings across forums. Lawyers who can shut down a frivolous proceeding early will be worth their weight in gold.

3. Making the attacker pay
Exemplary costs, malicious prosecution suits, defamation actions and perjury applications against false statements. Today these remedies are underused. When complaints become cheap, raising the cost for the person filing them becomes the main defensive strategy.

4. Regulatory and show-cause defence
Departments will use AI too. Expect more notices, more data-matched queries and more automated demands. Every one of them needs a human answer that will hold up.

5. Corporate whistleblower and POSH complaints
Internal complaints will get longer, more frequent and more legalistic. Companies will need lawyers to run inquiries that are fast, fair and defensible.

6. Triage and rebuttal at scale
The winning firms won't answer 900 pages with 900 pages. They'll use AI to map every allegation, find the contradictions, match each claim to documents and draft responses fast, and then put human judgment on the 5 allegations that actually matter.

The lawyers who will do best in the next decade aren't the ones who write the most. They're the ones who can look at 900 pages of plausible nonsense and say, "Only these 3 points are real. Here's how we kill the rest, and here's how we make them pay for it."

AI makes complaining trivial. It makes defending expensive, and that's where the work is going.

If you're a young lawyer in India, don't just learn to draft. Learn to defend: procedure, forum strategy, quashing, costs and cross-examination.

And use AI to answer at the same speed it's being used against your clients.

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.
